name: Straight photography
summary: A sharp, unmanipulated print of a real thing, made on a large camera at a small aperture. The beauty comes from the medium itself: fine detail, a long tonal scale and exact focus from front to back.

philosophy.core_thesis: Photography is an art of its own when it shows the world with the full detail and tonal range that only a camera can record.
design_principles: Stop down to f/32–f/64 on a view camera so that detail is sharp from the front to the horizon.
Previsualise the print: place the deepest shadow with detail on Zone III and the brightest textured highlight on Zone VII.
Fill the range: the print holds a true black (Dmax) and a clean paper white, with 8 to 10 steps between.
Choose a form that has its own pattern, such as a pepper, a dune or a shell, and fill the frame with it.
Print at full frame by contact, with no cropping, dodging beyond 1 stop or retouching.
Light the subject with clear, directional daylight at a ratio of 4:1 to 8:1 to model form.
anti_patterns: Soft-focus lenses, diffusion or brushed pigment
Tricks of the darkroom that change the scene, such as montage
Cropping a negative to rescue a weak composition
Muddy mid-grey prints with no true black or white
Warm sepia toning that hides the silver

composition.framing: Full-frame contact print; the format is 8×10 and the crop is the edge of the negative.
composition.viewpoint: Close and frontal on natural forms, or a clean distant view of a landscape at eye or tripod height.
composition.geometry: Strong patterns and repeated textures; edge-to-edge tonal balance, with no empty sky.
composition.subject_placement: Centred or filling the frame for objects; on a third for landscapes, with a clear foreground.

light.quality: Hard to medium, directional daylight that models form and shows texture.
light.direction: Side light at 45° to 90°, or soft light from a north window for still life.
light.time_of_day: Morning or late afternoon; midday only for still life in shade

lens_and_camera.format: 8×10 in or 4×5 in view camera, contact or enlarged print
lens_and_camera.focus: Tilt and swing to put the plane of sharp focus through the nearest and the farthest detail.
equipment: orange or red filter for skies

colour_and_grade.treatment: Neutral to slightly cool black-and-white on glossy silver gelatin paper, with a long scale and a true black.
grade_recipe: Convert to monochrome with an orange filter mix (R 70, G 30, B 0) to darken skies.
Set the black point at 2% and the white point at 97%.
Apply an S-curve of +25% midtone contrast.
Keep each of the zones from III to VII visible as a separate step.
Sharpen at radius 0.6px, amount 80%, once, at the output size.
Add no vignette, no tone and no texture.
colour_and_grade.grain: ISO 50–100 fine grain; invisible at 8×10 contact size

subject_and_staging.staging: Pick and place the subject with care; do not alter it. Clear the frame of anything that breaks the pattern.
subject_and_staging.direction: Still and unposed; portraits face the lens with a plain gaze.

workflow: Develop each negative by the Zone System, with N−1, N or N+1 times to fit the light.
Make a contact print on glossy or semi-matt silver gelatin paper.
Spot dust only; do not retouch the content.
Print to a clean white border, with the edge of the negative visible.
post_processing.output: A glossy, high-resolution print at 20 × 25 cm, shown flat in a plain white mat.

emotion.target_response: Clarity and respect: the viewer feels that the thing is shown as it is, and that it is worth looking at closely.

avoid_when: The brief needs a candid, moving subject or a quick snapshot feel.

modifiers.how: Open the aperture to f/8, add diffusion and a warm tone, and lift the black point to 15%; keep the large format and the quiet light.
Switch to a 35mm camera at f/8, shoot handheld and let the frame be found; keep the black and white and the strong light.

sources.title: Ansel Adams, The Negative (Little, Brown, 1981): the Zone System
Beaumont Newhall, The History of Photography (MoMA, 1982)
